title: The Cat, The Elf, and The Moonbeam
markdown:
The air in the High Peaks always tasted like melted snow and secrets. Far-off mule bells sang between jagged ridges. Moonlight, cold and bright, gathered on drifts like fallen stardust.

Elf Orryn stretched his arms wide. “Ah,” a soft puff against crisp air. “Today is for stillness. For the slow shift of shadows. For the silence between the wind’s whispers.”

It was not a day for stillness.

Beside him, Moss the pine marten chittered agreement, sleek fur blending with grey stone, whiskers a tiny engine of curiosity. A day, Moss thought, for sniffing wild thyme and the rustling lives among rocks.

The mountains had other plans. They were grand old things, and sometimes they liked to play pranks on those who thought they understood their moods.

A flurry of white tumbled down the slope with surprising speed and landed with a soft thud at Orryn’s feet: a rather plump cat. Nimbus, fur the colour of fresh snow, eyes twin emeralds, an almost aristocratic intelligence. He surveyed Orryn as if Orryn were slightly late.

“Greetings, Orryn of the Ridge,” Nimbus announced, a resonant purr that seemed to vibrate the ground. “Excellent. You’re punctual. A matter of utmost importance. Urgent. Matters of luminescence.”

Orryn stroked Moss. “Punctual? I was about to embark on quiet observation. The sort of day the mountains whisper for.”

“No time for preamble.” A perfectly groomed tail, a flourish that would make a courtier blush. “My client requires a delicate retrieval. A luminescent item. Quite rare. Currently misplaced, shall we say.”

Moss squeaked, nudging. Orryn ruffled him. “Your client? I don’t typically work for clients. I hire assistance. Mapping forgotten caves. Finding sunberries.”

Nimbus tilted his head, feline dignity only slightly undermined by being, fundamentally, a cat. “Consider this a fortunate misunderstanding. You are hired. Compensation will be adequate. More than adequate. The sun descends. Shadows lengthen. Time is a particularly elusive butterfly.”

A mountain grumble started in Orryn’s chest. Moss’s tail flicked, excited. This was no longer stillness. This was an ambush, and he was, rather unexpectedly, willing.

“Alright, Nimbus. Tell me about the luminescent item. Specific, if you please. I’m not fond of chasing moonbeams without knowing why.”

Nimbus preened. “It’s called a moonbeam. A particularly fine specimen. Potent, even nascent. We must catch it before it dissipates. My client is terribly anxious. Follow me!” The white cat trotted off without waiting, improbable grace, a living shadow on rugged ground.

It was not a day for stillness.

Higher they went, along narrow goat paths where the only sound was the sharp crunch of boots on scree and the rhythmic panting of Moss, who seemed to be enjoying the chase immensely. Nimbus, surprisingly agile for his plump build, bounded ahead, occasionally pausing to give a series of cryptic meows and ear twitches that Orryn, with keen elven senses honed by years of mountain living, somehow understood as directions.

“Left at the twisted pine, the one that looks like it’s forever reaching for a forgotten star,” Nimbus would say through pointed ears and tail flicks. “Then right at the screaming rock — you’ll know it by the wind’s mournful cry when it passes through the crevices. And for goodness sake, try not to step on any whistling marmots; they’re terribly sensitive.” Orryn found himself chuckling. It was certainly a different sort of quest than he’d anticipated. He’d expected to be cataloguing rare mosses, not deciphering feline directions.

They clambered over boulders slick with early frost, their surfaces glinting like forgotten jewels. They navigated patches of stubborn snow that clung to the north-facing slopes like stubborn barnacles on a ship’s hull. At one point, Nimbus, attempting to leap a chasm that Orryn himself had calculated with a practiced eye, misjudged the distance and landed with a comical splooosh in a shallow, icy puddle at the bottom. He emerged, looking thoroughly disgruntled, shaking water everywhere like a tiny, angry fountain.

“Honestly,” he huffed, his voice a tiny hiss of annoyance, “the indignity! If you'd had the proper equipment, this wouldn't have happened. A properly equipped explorer never gets wet paws, you know.”

Orryn wiped stray drops. “A lesson,” he whispered to Moss, who watched with wide amused eyes. “Never assume a cat can judge distance over water. Their minds are on the exact shape of a sunbeam, or the philosophy of an empty bowl.”

Twilight rose, rose and amethyst and fiery orange. A high secluded plateau. A magnificent waterfall; spray catching last sun, a fleeting rainbow. Nestled in a crystalline bowl, positioned to catch dwindling day and the first shy moon: a shimmering ethereal ribbon. Pulsed, pearly, not quite solid, not quite air — spun moonlight on spider-silk. A captured moonbeam, more delicate than anything Orryn had catalogued.

“There!” Nimbus puffed. “Magnificent. My client is a rather shy Moon-Sprite. She collects them. Quiet light is a balm. She accidentally trapped this one practising light-weaving. Distressed. Wringing tiny hands, which is rather difficult when you have no hands, but she managed admirably.”

Orryn stared, observational calm replaced by wonder. Aurora, ancient ferns, a glimpse of snow leopard — never a captured beam of pure light. Nimbus nudged it with his nose as if stroking a jewel. Stern demeanor softened into palpable affection.

“You did all this for a Moon-Sprite? A lost beam of light?”

“Of course.” Emerald eyes catching glow. “Friendship is a precious thing. It transcends inconvenience, and the occasional unplanned bath. Even unconventional hiring. She is a dear friend. Her happiness is of paramount importance.”

Warmth spread through Orryn, more satisfying than solitary contemplation. The quiet day was ruined, magnificently. Moss watched the moonbeam vibrating with silent awe.

Orryn approached the bowl. Not to capture. Not to possess. To release. A finger-tip, light as a falling feather. The moonbeam detached with a silent silvery shimmer, flowed upward, caught the first true rays of a moon like a pearl in indigo. It danced, twirled, leapt, merged with the waterfall. The cascade became liquid silver pouring from the stars, painting rock with ethereal transient glow.

“Oh, thank you!” Nimbus chirped, unpretentious, better than his earlier pronouncements. “She will be so pleased. She was on the verge of a rather mournful ballad about lost light.”

Down the mountain, path in familiar moon. Orryn’s stillness had been hijacked, and contentment sat in his chest anyway. He had helped a friend, feline and sprite, and seen a beauty that would not need cataloguing.

As they neared the village, the cheerful sound of laughter and music drifted up to meet them, a warm invitation. The villagers were holding their annual Starlight Festival, a cozy gathering where oil lamps cast warm pools of light, chasing away shadows, and the sweet spicy scent of mulled cider filled the air. Orryn, Moss, and Nimbus joined the throng. Orryn shared a mug of cider, its warmth a welcome contrast to the mountain chill. Moss nibbled contentedly on a bit of dried berry cake, his tail wagging with delight. And Nimbus, surprisingly, seemed quite content to sit by Orryn’s feet, occasionally purring a soft melody that seemed to echo the gentle chime of the distant mule bells.

Today had not been for stillness. The bells went on singing. The peaks kept their snow. The waterfall, somewhere above, kept a little extra silver, and Orryn, who had meant only to watch shadows, found that watching a cat hire him had been, all things considered, an acceptable trade.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
